topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: If an Ohio real estate brokerage is organized as a corporation, what does R.C. 4735.08 require regarding the corporation's officers?
choice_a: The officers of the corporation who actively participate in the brokerage business must themselves hold real estate broker's licenses
choice_b: Corporate officers are categorically exempt from licensure because the corporation itself holds the brokerage license
choice_c: Only the corporation's president must be licensed; other officers are exempt regardless of their role
choice_d: Corporations are prohibited from operating as real estate brokerages in Ohio
explanation: R.C. 4735.08 extends the same entity-level licensure principle applied to partnerships to corporations: officers who actively participate in the brokerage's real estate business must themselves hold broker's licenses, so that active control of a brokerage carries a personal licensure obligation regardless of the entity form chosen.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage incorporates, and its vice president actively manages listings, negotiates transactions, and supervises salespersons, but has never obtained an Ohio broker's license. Does this comply with R.C. 4735.08?
choice_a: No, because an officer who actively participates in the brokerage business must hold a broker's license, regardless of title
choice_b: Yes, because only the corporation's registered agent is required to be licensed
choice_c: Yes, because corporate officers are automatically covered by the corporation's own entity-level license
choice_d: Yes, provided the vice president discloses their unlicensed status to clients in writing
explanation: R.C. 4735.08's entity-compliance requirement turns on active participation in the brokerage business, not job title -- an unlicensed vice president who is actually managing listings, negotiating, and supervising licensees would not satisfy the statute merely because someone else in the corporation happens to hold a license.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A real estate brokerage is organized as a limited liability company (LLC). Under the entity-compliance principle reflected in R.C. 4735.08, what is generally required of the LLC's members?
choice_a: Members who actively participate in conducting the brokerage's real estate business must themselves hold broker's licenses
choice_b: No member of an LLC brokerage is ever required to be licensed, because the LLC's license covers all members automatically
choice_c: Only the LLC's registered statutory agent must be licensed
choice_d: LLC members are exempt from licensure as long as the LLC maintains liability insurance
explanation: Ohio's entity-level licensure principle applies across business-entity forms used to operate a brokerage: members of an LLC who actively participate in the brokerage's real estate business must hold broker's licenses, mirroring the treatment applied to partners and corporate officers under R.C. 4735.08.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: An investor holds a passive, non-managing membership interest in a brokerage organized as an LLC, contributing capital but never participating in listing, negotiating, or supervising real estate transactions. Does this passive investor's lack of a broker's license, by itself, violate the entity-compliance principle behind R.C. 4735.08?
choice_a: Generally no, because the licensure requirement targets members who actively participate in conducting the brokerage's real estate business, not merely passive capital investors
choice_b: Yes, because every member of a licensed brokerage entity must be a broker regardless of their role
choice_c: Yes, but only if the passive investor's ownership share exceeds 50 percent
choice_d: No, because LLCs are entirely exempt from R.C. 4735.08's entity-compliance requirements
explanation: The entity-compliance principle is tied to active participation in the brokerage's real estate business; a purely passive investor who contributes capital without directing or conducting brokerage activity does not, by that fact alone, trigger the same licensure obligation as an actively participating partner, officer, or member.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What does R.C. 4735.13 require regarding a brokerage's physical operations in Ohio?
choice_a: A brokerage must maintain a definite, identifiable place of business, and the broker's license must be prominently displayed there
choice_b: A brokerage may operate entirely without any fixed office location, using only a post office box for all licensing purposes
choice_c: A brokerage's place of business need not be disclosed to the Ohio Division of Real Estate and Professional Licensing
choice_d: License display requirements apply only to branch offices, not to a brokerage's main office
explanation: R.C. 4735.13 requires a brokerage to maintain a definite place of business and to display its broker's license there, ensuring the public and the Division can identify a fixed, accountable location where the brokerage conducts its licensed business.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage operates solely through a rented mailbox and conducts all client meetings at coffee shops or clients' homes, with no fixed office of its own. Does this satisfy R.C. 4735.13's definite-place-of-business requirement?
choice_a: No, because a mailbox alone does not constitute the definite, identifiable place of business the statute requires
choice_b: Yes, because Ohio law does not require any physical location at all for a licensed brokerage
choice_c: Yes, as long as the brokerage's website lists a business address
choice_d: No, but only because coffee shops are not zoned for commercial use
explanation: R.C. 4735.13's definite-place-of-business requirement contemplates an actual, identifiable office location where the brokerage's license can be displayed and its business conducted -- a mailbox alone, without any fixed office, would not satisfy that requirement.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.13, if a brokerage wants to open a branch office at a second location, what is generally required?
choice_a: The branch office must be separately licensed and must have a licensed broker or qualified management-level licensee supervising it
choice_b: No separate licensing or supervision is required for branch offices, since the brokerage's main-office license covers every location
choice_c: Branch offices are prohibited outright under Ohio real estate law
choice_d: A branch office may operate under supervision from the main office by phone only, with no on-site licensed supervisor required
explanation: R.C. 4735.13 requires a brokerage's branch office to be separately licensed and to have a licensed broker or qualified management-level licensee responsible for its supervision, extending the accountability and oversight structure that applies to a brokerage's main office to each additional location.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage opens a second full-service office across town, staffs it with several salespersons, and begins taking listings there, but never obtains a separate branch-office license for that location. What is the compliance problem under R.C. 4735.13?
choice_a: The brokerage has failed to obtain the separate branch-office license the statute requires for an additional business location conducting real estate business
choice_b: There is no compliance problem, because a single brokerage license automatically covers unlimited additional office locations
choice_c: The problem is only that the new office lacks its own separate corporate charter
choice_d: The problem exists only if the second office is located in a different county than the main office
explanation: Because R.C. 4735.13 requires each branch office conducting a brokerage's real estate business to be separately licensed, opening and staffing an additional full-service office without obtaining that separate license would leave the location out of compliance, regardless of whether it is in the same or a different county.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.13, when a salesperson's or broker's association with a brokerage terminates, what notice timeframe applies?
choice_a: Notice of the termination must generally be given within 3 business days
choice_b: No notice of any kind is ever required when a licensee's association with a brokerage ends
choice_c: Notice must be given within 6 months of the termination taking effect
choice_d: Notice is required only if the terminated licensee objects to leaving the brokerage
explanation: R.C. 4735.13 attaches a short, specific notice window -- generally 3 business days -- to the termination of a licensee's association with a brokerage, so that licensure records accurately and promptly reflect where an active licensee is affiliated.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.13, if a brokerage relocates its place of business to a new address, what notice period generally applies?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 3 business days, identical to the departure-notice window for an individual licensee
choice_c: No notice is required as long as the brokerage's phone number stays the same
choice_d: 1 full calendar year
explanation: R.C. 4735.13 sets a 30-day notice window for a brokerage's relocation of its place of business, a longer timeframe than the shorter 3-business-day window that applies to notifying the termination of an individual licensee's association with a brokerage.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage moves its main office to a new building across town in early January but does not notify the Division of the relocation until late April. Under R.C. 4735.13's relocation-notice requirement, what is the compliance issue?
choice_a: The brokerage exceeded the 30-day window generally required for notifying the Division of a relocation
choice_b: There is no compliance issue, because relocation notice is purely optional under Ohio law
choice_c: The brokerage only needed to update its own website, not notify the Division at all
choice_d: The compliance issue is that the brokerage should have closed for the entire moving period
explanation: Because R.C. 4735.13 generally requires relocation notice within 30 days, waiting roughly four months to notify the Division of a change of address would fall well outside that statutory window.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.16, what must a brokerage's advertising generally include?
choice_a: The brokerage's own licensed name, so that the advertising cannot be mistaken as coming from an unaffiliated or unlicensed source
choice_b: A full listing of every other property currently for sale by the brokerage, regardless of relevance
choice_c: The personal home address of the supervising broker
choice_d: A statement that the advertised property has never been previously listed with any other brokerage
explanation: R.C. 4735.16 requires that real estate advertising disclose the brokerage under whose license the advertising is placed, ensuring consumers can identify the responsible licensed brokerage behind any given ad rather than being left to guess who is actually offering the property.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.16, what disclosure is required when a licensee advertises property in which the licensee personally holds an ownership interest?
choice_a: The advertising must disclose the licensee's ownership interest, commonly satisfied by an "agent owned" or equivalent disclosure
choice_b: No disclosure is required as long as the licensee uses a personal name rather than the brokerage's name in the ad
choice_c: The licensee must have the property appraised by an independent appraiser before any advertising may run
choice_d: Disclosure is required only if the licensee's ownership interest exceeds 50 percent of the property
explanation: R.C. 4735.16 requires a licensee advertising property in which they hold an ownership interest to disclose that interest, typically through an "agent owned" or similarly worded notice, so that prospective buyers understand they may be dealing with a licensee acting in a self-interested capacity rather than a neutral listing agent.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A salesperson lists their own personal vacation condo for sale through their brokerage and runs newspaper ads for it that make no mention of the salesperson's ownership interest. What R.C. 4735.16 problem does this create?
choice_a: The ad fails to include the "agent owned" (or equivalent) disclosure R.C. 4735.16 requires when a licensee has an ownership interest in the advertised property
choice_b: There is no problem, because a licensee's own property is exempt from all advertising disclosure requirements
choice_c: The only problem is that the brokerage's name was included in the ad
choice_d: The ad would only be problematic if the condo were priced above the county's median home value
explanation: Because R.C. 4735.16 requires disclosure of a licensee's ownership interest in property being advertised, an ad for the salesperson's own condo that omits any mention of that interest fails to satisfy the statute's "agent owned" (or equivalent) disclosure requirement.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.16, may a brokerage advertise a property it currently has under an active listing agreement as "for sale by owner"?
choice_a: No -- R.C. 4735.16 prohibits advertising a listed property as "for sale by owner"
choice_b: Yes, as long as the seller personally requests the "for sale by owner" wording in writing
choice_c: Yes, provided the brokerage's commission on the sale is reduced by half
choice_d: Yes, but only for properties listed for more than 90 days without an offer
explanation: R.C. 4735.16 specifically prohibits advertising a currently listed property as "for sale by owner," because that characterization misleads the public about whether a licensed brokerage is actually representing the seller in the transaction.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A brokerage runs online ads for a property under an active listing agreement, labeling it "for sale by owner -- no agent fees" in an effort to attract buyers looking to avoid working with an agent. What is the R.C. 4735.16 problem with this advertising?
choice_a: It violates R.C. 4735.16's prohibition on advertising a listed property as "for sale by owner"
choice_b: There is no problem, because the ad's goal of attracting more buyers justifies the wording used
choice_c: The only issue is that the ad does not mention the property's square footage
choice_d: The ad would be permissible if run for fewer than 7 days
explanation: Because the property is actually under an active listing agreement with the brokerage, labeling it "for sale by owner" -- regardless of the marketing rationale -- directly violates R.C. 4735.16's prohibition on that specific mischaracterization.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under R.C. 4735.16, what is the maximum civil fine that may generally be imposed per citation for a violation of the statute's advertising requirements?
choice_a: Up to $2,500 per citation
choice_b: Up to $100 per citation, regardless of the violation's severity
choice_c: There is no monetary fine available under R.C. 4735.16 -- only license revocation
choice_d: Up to $250,000 per citation
explanation: R.C. 4735.16 authorizes a civil fine of up to $2,500 per citation for advertising violations, giving the Division a monetary enforcement tool for advertising noncompliance separate from the broader disciplinary process under R.C. 4735.18.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: How does the enforcement mechanism for an R.C. 4735.16 advertising violation generally differ from the broader license-discipline process under R.C. 4735.18?
choice_a: R.C. 4735.16 authorizes a specific civil fine (up to $2,500 per citation) targeted at advertising violations, while R.C. 4735.18 provides the general disciplinary framework covering a much broader range of licensee misconduct
choice_b: The two statutes are functionally identical and cannot be applied to different conduct
choice_c: R.C. 4735.16 can only be enforced through criminal prosecution, never a civil fine
choice_d: R.C. 4735.18 applies only to advertising misconduct, while R.C. 4735.16 covers all other disciplinable conduct
explanation: R.C. 4735.16 supplies a targeted civil-fine mechanism (up to $2,500 per citation) specifically for advertising noncompliance, while R.C. 4735.18(A) supplies the much broader catalog of disciplinable conduct -- misrepresentation, undisclosed dual roles, unauthorized listings, and dozens of other grounds -- that can trigger the Commission's general disciplinary authority, including for advertising-related misconduct that also happens to be misleading or inaccurate under (A)(21).

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Among common business-entity structures, what generally distinguishes a limited partnership (LP) from a general partnership with respect to partner liability?
choice_a: A limited partnership has at least one general partner with unlimited personal liability, while its limited partners generally have liability restricted to their capital investment, so long as they do not participate in management
choice_b: All partners in a limited partnership, without exception, have unlimited personal liability identical to a general partnership
choice_c: A limited partnership cannot have more than one partner total
choice_d: Limited partners in a limited partnership are always personally liable for the full amount of the partnership's debts regardless of their role
explanation: Under general business-entity doctrine, a limited partnership structure separates roles: at least one general partner retains unlimited personal liability and management authority, while limited partners generally enjoy liability limited to their investment, provided they refrain from actively managing the business -- a distinction not present in an ordinary general partnership, where every partner is typically fully liable.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: From a general business-entity taxation standpoint, what is a key distinction commonly drawn between an S corporation and a C corporation?
choice_a: An S corporation generally passes income through to shareholders' personal tax returns without entity-level federal income tax, while a C corporation is generally subject to corporate-level income tax, creating potential double taxation when profits are also distributed as dividends
choice_b: A C corporation is always taxed at a lower rate than an S corporation under all circumstances
choice_c: There is no meaningful tax distinction between an S corporation and a C corporation
choice_d: Only a C corporation can have shareholders; an S corporation cannot be owned by anyone
explanation: General business-taxation doctrine treats an S corporation as a pass-through entity for federal income tax purposes, avoiding entity-level tax, while a C corporation is generally taxed on its own income, with shareholders then also taxed again on dividend distributions -- the double-taxation dynamic commonly cited as a key structural difference between the two corporate tax elections.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What does the general business-law concept of "piercing the corporate veil" refer to?
choice_a: A court disregarding a corporation's or LLC's separate legal existence and holding an owner personally liable, typically where corporate formalities were ignored, the entity was undercapitalized, or the entity form was used to commit fraud or injustice
choice_b: The routine, automatic process by which a corporation is formed under state law
choice_c: A tax election available only to sole proprietorships
choice_d: A method for a corporation to increase its number of authorized shares
explanation: "Piercing the corporate veil" is the general business-law doctrine under which a court sets aside the normal liability shield of a corporation or LLC and holds an owner personally responsible for entity debts or misconduct, typically triggered by failure to observe corporate formalities, commingling of personal and business assets, undercapitalization, or use of the entity to perpetrate fraud.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Many real estate brokerages operate under a well-known national franchise brand name. From a general business-entity standpoint, what does that franchise relationship typically mean for the local brokerage's legal structure?
choice_a: The local brokerage is typically still its own independently owned and operated legal entity that has licensed the right to use the franchisor's brand, systems, and marketing, rather than being owned or operated by the national franchisor itself
choice_b: A franchise brand automatically merges every local office into one single national legal entity with shared liability
choice_c: Franchised brokerages are exempt from state real estate licensure requirements because of their franchise affiliation
choice_d: The national franchisor is automatically the principal broker of record for every local franchised office
explanation: As a matter of general business-entity structure, a real estate franchise arrangement is typically a licensing relationship: the local brokerage remains its own independently owned and operated legal entity (often an LLC or corporation) that pays for the right to use the franchisor's brand and systems, while still being separately responsible for its own state real estate licensure, including designating its own principal broker.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: In general agency and fiduciary-duty doctrine as applied to real estate brokerage, what set of core duties does an agent typically owe to the principal (client) they represent?
choice_a: Obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care and skill
choice_b: Only the duty to close the transaction as quickly as possible, regardless of the client's other interests
choice_c: No fiduciary duties at all, since a real estate agent is treated purely as an independent contractor with no duties to the client
choice_d: A single, generic duty of "good faith" that supersedes and replaces all other specific fiduciary obligations
explanation: Standard fiduciary-duty doctrine applied to real estate agency recognizes a cluster of core duties an agent owes a principal -- commonly summarized as obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care and skill -- each addressing a different dimension of the trust relationship between agent and client.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within the fiduciary duties an agent owes a principal, what does the duty of loyalty specifically require?
choice_a: The agent must act in the principal's best interest, avoiding self-dealing or placing the agent's own interests, or a third party's interests, ahead of the client's
choice_b: The agent must always follow every instruction from the principal even when doing so would be illegal
choice_c: The agent must disclose the principal's confidential financial information to any third party who requests it
choice_d: The agent has no obligation to disclose a personal financial interest in a transaction as long as the deal still closes
explanation: The duty of loyalty is centrally about avoiding conflicts between the agent's interests and the client's: an agent must act in the principal's best interest and refrain from self-dealing or favoring their own (or a third party's) financial interest over the client's, distinguishing loyalty from the separate duty of obedience, which is bounded by legal and ethical limits.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within the fiduciary duties an agent owes a principal, what does the duty of confidentiality generally protect?
choice_a: The principal's sensitive information -- such as motivation to sell, financial position, or negotiating limits -- which the agent must not disclose to the other side of a transaction without authorization, and which can continue to apply even after the agency relationship ends
choice_b: Only information that is already publicly available through the multiple listing service
choice_c: Confidentiality applies exclusively to written communications and never to information learned verbally
choice_d: Confidentiality obligations end automatically the moment a purchase agreement is signed, regardless of what information remains sensitive
explanation: The duty of confidentiality generally protects sensitive information the agent learns in the course of representing the principal -- such as the client's true motivation, financial limits, or negotiating position -- from disclosure to the other party without authorization, and this protection can, as a matter of general agency doctrine, continue to apply even after the formal agency relationship has ended.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within the fiduciary duties an agent owes a principal, what does the duty of disclosure generally require regarding material facts?
choice_a: The agent must disclose material facts relevant to the transaction that affect the principal's decision-making, such as facts bearing on a property's value or desirability that the agent knows or reasonably should know
choice_b: The agent has no obligation to disclose any facts to the principal beyond the purchase price
choice_c: Disclosure obligations run only to the other party in the transaction, never to the agent's own principal
choice_d: The duty of disclosure is satisfied automatically simply by using a standardized purchase contract form
explanation: The duty of disclosure requires an agent to keep the principal informed of material facts bearing on the transaction -- information affecting the property's value, desirability, or the client's decision-making -- reflecting the general fiduciary expectation that a principal be given the information needed to make informed decisions.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within the fiduciary duties an agent owes a principal, what does the duty of reasonable care and skill generally require of a real estate licensee?
choice_a: The agent must perform the tasks of the representation competently, applying the knowledge, skill, and diligence that would reasonably be expected of a licensed real estate professional
choice_b: The agent is held to no professional standard at all and cannot be found negligent under any circumstances
choice_c: The duty of reasonable care applies only to licensees who have practiced for more than ten years
choice_d: The duty is fully satisfied as long as the transaction eventually closes, regardless of how it was handled along the way
explanation: The duty of reasonable care and skill is a competence-based fiduciary obligation: it requires the agent to bring the knowledge, diligence, and professional skill reasonably expected of a licensed real estate practitioner to the tasks undertaken on the principal's behalf, independent of whether a given transaction happens to close successfully.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within the fiduciary duties an agent owes a principal, what does the duty of accounting generally require?
choice_a: The agent must properly account for and safeguard all funds, documents, and property entrusted by or on behalf of the principal in connection with the transaction
choice_b: The agent must prepare and file the principal's personal federal income tax return
choice_c: The duty of accounting applies only to commercial transactions, never to residential ones
choice_d: The agent has no obligation to track or report what happens to client funds once they are deposited
explanation: The duty of accounting requires an agent to properly handle, safeguard, and be able to report on funds, documents, and property received in connection with a principal's transaction -- a duty that also underlies the specific trust-account handling and recordkeeping obligations imposed by Ohio license law.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: As a matter of general ethical practice, when does a real estate licensee facing a potential conflict of interest generally need to disclose that conflict?
choice_a: As soon as the licensee becomes aware of a fact or relationship that could compromise their objectivity or loyalty, so that any affected party can make an informed decision about how to proceed
choice_b: Only after the transaction has already closed
choice_c: Only if a party specifically asks the licensee, in those exact words, whether a conflict exists
choice_d: Disclosure of conflicts of interest is never ethically required in real estate practice
explanation: General ethical practice for real estate licensees calls for prompt disclosure of a potential conflict of interest as soon as it becomes apparent, since timely disclosure is what allows an affected client or party to make an informed decision about whether and how to proceed, rather than discovering the conflict only after commitments have already been made.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate ethics doctrine

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: How does a voluntary professional code of ethics, such as one maintained by a real estate trade association, generally differ from Ohio's statutory license-law discipline framework under R.C. 4735.18?
choice_a: A voluntary code of ethics is generally enforced by the professional association itself against its own members, while R.C. 4735.18 is the state's statutory disciplinary authority enforced by the Ohio Real Estate Commission against any licensee, whether or not they belong to the association
choice_b: A voluntary trade-association code of ethics and Ohio's statutory license law are legally identical and enforced by the same body
choice_c: Only association members are subject to any form of real estate professional discipline in Ohio
choice_d: R.C. 4735.18 applies only to association members, while non-members are exempt from all discipline
explanation: A trade association's code of ethics is a voluntary, membership-based standard enforced internally by that association against its own members, whereas R.C. 4735.18 is Ohio's statutory disciplinary framework, enforced by the state Real Estate Commission against any licensee regardless of trade-association membership -- two distinct accountability systems that can overlap in substance but differ in source and enforcement authority.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate ethics doctrine, cross-referenced with ORC 4735.18

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine (rooted in the federal Sherman Antitrust Act) as it applies to real estate practice, what conduct among competing brokerages is generally prohibited?
choice_a: Agreements between competing brokerages that unreasonably restrain trade, such as fixing prices, allocating markets, or engaging in group boycotts
choice_b: Any competition at all between real estate brokerages, since antitrust law is understood to require brokerages to cooperate on pricing
choice_c: Advertising a brokerage's own commission rates to the public
choice_d: A brokerage independently deciding, without coordinating with competitors, what commission rate to charge its own clients
explanation: General antitrust doctrine, rooted in the Sherman Antitrust Act, prohibits agreements among competitors that unreasonably restrain trade -- including price fixing, market or customer allocation, and group boycotts -- while an individual brokerage's own independent pricing and advertising decisions, made without coordinating with competitors, are not themselves antitrust violations.
source_note: hedge: standard antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine, why is an agreement among competing brokers to all charge the same commission rate treated as particularly serious antitrust conduct?
choice_a: Price fixing among competitors is generally treated as a per se antitrust violation -- meaning it is presumed illegal without needing to separately prove actual anticompetitive market effects
choice_b: It is not treated as a violation at all, because commission rates are set by state law rather than by individual brokers
choice_c: It only becomes a violation if fewer than three brokerages participate in the agreement
choice_d: Antitrust law applies exclusively to manufacturing industries and does not reach services such as real estate brokerage
explanation: Horizontal price fixing among competitors -- agreeing on the prices (here, commission rates) each will charge -- is a classic category of conduct treated under general antitrust doctrine as a per se violation, meaning courts presume it unlawful without requiring separate proof of actual market harm, precisely because of how directly it undermines independent, competitive pricing.
source_note: hedge: standard antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: At an informal gathering, several competing local brokers agree among themselves that none of them will charge a commission below a certain percentage, regardless of what any individual client negotiates. Under general antitrust doctrine, what is the legal problem with this agreement?
choice_a: It constitutes horizontal price fixing among competitors, a per se antitrust violation, regardless of how informally the agreement was reached
choice_b: There is no legal problem, because the agreement was informal and not put in writing
choice_c: The agreement is lawful as long as each broker still independently advertises a different rate to the public
choice_d: The agreement is lawful because commission rates are always negotiable regardless of any such agreement
explanation: Under general antitrust doctrine, the informality of an agreement among competitors does not shield it from liability -- a group of competing brokers agreeing to a minimum commission floor is horizontal price fixing, a per se antitrust violation, whether the agreement is written, verbal, or simply an informal understanding reached at a social gathering.
source_note: hedge: standard antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine, what does "market allocation" among competing brokerages refer to, and why is it prohibited?
choice_a: An agreement among competing brokerages to divide up geographic territories or types of clients between themselves, which is prohibited because it eliminates the competition that would otherwise exist between them in the allocated areas
choice_b: A brokerage's own internal decision about which neighborhoods its agents will focus their marketing efforts on
choice_c: A government program that assigns specific market territories to individual brokerages by regulation
choice_d: Market allocation refers to permissible competition on price within a defined geographic area
explanation: Market allocation is an agreement among competitors to divide up territories, customer types, or market segments rather than competing for the same business -- like price fixing, it is generally prohibited under antitrust doctrine because it eliminates competition that would otherwise exist between the colluding competitors within the allocated areas, distinct from a single brokerage's own unilateral marketing-focus decisions.
source_note: hedge: standard antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine, what is a "group boycott," and how might it arise among competing real estate brokerages?
choice_a: An agreement among competitors to collectively refuse to deal with, or to disadvantage, another business -- such as several established brokerages agreeing to deny a discount brokerage access to cooperative showings or referrals
choice_b: A single brokerage's independent decision not to cooperate with one particular competitor for legitimate business reasons unrelated to any agreement with others
choice_c: A government-mandated boycott of brokerages that violate consumer-protection law
choice_d: A marketing technique in which a brokerage temporarily lowers its prices to attract more clients
explanation: A group boycott, in antitrust doctrine, is a coordinated agreement among multiple competitors to collectively refuse to deal with or otherwise disadvantage a targeted business -- for example, several traditional brokerages agreeing among themselves to exclude a discount brokerage from cooperative referrals or showings -- which is treated as antitrust conduct precisely because it is a coordinated agreement rather than any one firm's independent business decision.
source_note: hedge: standard antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine, what antitrust concern can arise from a "tying arrangement," such as a brokerage requiring a seller to use its affiliated title or mortgage company as a condition of accepting a listing?
choice_a: Conditioning one service on the mandatory purchase of a separate, distinct service can raise antitrust concerns by improperly leveraging market power in one service to restrict competition in the other
choice_b: Tying arrangements are always fully lawful under antitrust law regardless of the circumstances
choice_c: Tying concerns apply only to manufactured goods, never to services such as title or mortgage services
choice_d: A brokerage merely recommending, without requiring, an affiliated service provider is automatically an antitrust violation
explanation: A tying arrangement -- conditioning the sale or provision of one product or service on the mandatory purchase of a separate, distinct one -- can raise antitrust concerns when it leverages market power to restrict competition in the tied service, which is why merely recommending (rather than requiring) an affiliated provider is treated very differently under antitrust doctrine than making that provider's use a mandatory condition.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general antitrust doctrine, is it lawful for an individual brokerage to independently set its own commission rates without any coordination with competing brokerages?
choice_a: Yes -- each brokerage independently setting its own rates, without agreement or coordination with competitors, is standard lawful competitive conduct; the antitrust concern arises specifically from agreements between competitors, not from independent pricing decisions
choice_b: No -- any brokerage setting its own commission rate at all is automatically an antitrust violation
choice_c: It is lawful only if every brokerage in the state happens to end up charging an identical rate
choice_d: It is lawful only if the rate is submitted in advance to the Ohio Division of Real Estate and Professional Licensing for approval
explanation: Antitrust doctrine targets agreements or coordination between competitors, not the independent pricing decisions any single business makes on its own -- a brokerage is free to set its own commission rates unilaterally, and that independent conduct remains lawful even if, coincidentally, other brokerages end up charging similar rates through their own separate decisions.
